tagline: Switchbacks to the James River, where an old bridge forks
intro: Between Reeds Spring and Galena, three route numbers share one winding, hilly road: Routes 248, 265 and 413. This two-lane stretch makes switchbacks through the Ozarks and has no-passing stripes throughout. The Missouri Department of Transportation includes the Ozark Mountain Parkway on its scenic-byways roster as Route 265 in Stone County.

At Galena, the road’s history takes the shape of a letter. The Y-Bridge opened over the James River in 1927 to carry Routes 13 and 44, now numbered 413 and 248. Its east end split so drivers could turn north or south where the highway was confined between a steep bluff and the river. A newer crossing to the north now carries traffic. Route 413 follows an older alignment of Route 13, which was later rerouted. Route 265 shares much of its length with other numbered highways.

From Branson West, Routes 265 and 413 head north through mountainous country to Reeds Spring. Route 248 joins them for the winding approach to Galena and the James River crossing. Route 248 leaves the shared road at Galena. Beyond Galena, Routes 265 and 413 continue through farmland, pass Elsey and a dense forest, and reach Crane.

moments.title: Reeds Spring
moments.text: The name Reeds Spring began with a farm beside a spring. Fitzhugh Reed settled near the original town site and called his farm Reed’s Springs; the town was formally organized in 1906. Here Route 248 joins Routes 265 and 413 for the winding two-lane drive toward Galena.

moments.title: Y-Bridge
moments.text: Galena’s Y-Bridge made a junction out of a river crossing. Opened in 1927, it carried Routes 13 and 44 over the James River. At the east end, drivers could choose a northbound or southbound branch, fitting the highway into the space between a steep bluff and the water. Those routes are now numbered 413 and 248. The old bridge is on the National Register of Historic Places, while a newer bridge to its north carries vehicles across the river. The old crossing’s three branches give the bridge its name and distinctive outline.
moments.notice: The east end divides into two branches between the bluff and river.

moments.title: Crane
moments.text: Crane took its name from the creek when the town was platted in 1895. The stream runs through town and belongs to the James River system, part of the larger White River drainage. Past Crane’s southwest side, it flows beneath Route 13, then turns east past Quail and south of Hurley before bending southeast toward the James. The creek is classified as a Blue Ribbon Trout Area in the Missouri Department of Conservation’s trout management program. The stream runs for 23.2 miles; its name refers to the blue cranes in the area.

practical: Y-Bridge: The Y-Bridge is closed to vehicles; the newer bridge to the north carries road traffic. (checked 2026-10-11)
